steps.message: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Let's add a new feature—bots. Bots can be members of rooms and post messages via an HTTP API.

Any chat member can create and manage bots via the user interface:
- open the account settings page (`/account/edit`)
- click the bot icon ("Set up chat bots")

This opens the bots page (`/bots`). It lists the bots you created (administrators see all bots) and has the "Add a chat bot" button. The button opens the `/bots/new` page with a form:

- bot avatar (optional)
- bot name (required), labelled "Name the bot"
- the "Save changes" button

Submitting the form creates a bot and redirects back to `/bots`. Each bot on the list shows its name and its unique bot code in a read-only field labelled "Bot code", in the same list item—the code is used to authenticate bot requests. The bot code is a sensitive credential. The bots page shows all of your bots on one page, without pagination.

From the list, you can also edit a bot (name, avatar): each bot has an "Edit <bot name>" link (for example, "Edit Deploy Bot") to its edit page. The edit page uses the same form and has a "Delete this chat bot" button that asks for confirmation. A deleted bot can no longer post messages.

Like any new user, a new bot joins all open rooms. Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people.

Here is how a bot can post a message:

```
curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \
  https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages
```

Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names.

The endpoint responds with:

- `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`
- `422 Unprocessable Content` — empty body and no attachment
- `404 Not Found` — bad room id
- `401 Unauthorized` — invalid bot code

The message is broadcast to connected clients and triggers push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would.

The message shows the bot (its name) as the author.

steps.message: Let's inspect the directory contents of `docs`, `app`, `config/routes.rb`, `db/schema.rb`, and `test` to understand the models, controllers, views, and tests.
steps.reasoning_content:
Okay, here's my take on those "thoughts," tailored for an expert audience:

**Diving Deep: A Reconnaissance Mission**

Right, so we're starting fresh, I see. My initial instinct, as always, is to get a lay of the land. We need a solid understanding of the project's structure and key components before we even think about touching any code. Therefore, my first move is reconnaissance. Let's start with a systematic sweep: I'm mentally parsing the obvious suspects.

`docs/` is the first stop, of course. I'm hoping for some high-level architecture diagrams, maybe some API documentation, or at the very least, some READMEs to get me oriented. Anything that demystifies the overall design or provides a roadmap is gold.

Next, I'm heading directly to `db/schema.rb`. This is the ground truth. I want to understand the data model: the tables, the relationships, the constraints. I'm looking for clues about the underlying business logic reflected in the data. Any database design decisions I can observe will save me time later.

`config/routes.rb` is crucial. The routing file paints the broad strokes of how the application exposes its functionality. I'm mentally mapping the URLs to controllers and actions. What's the application surface area? How are the different features connected from a user perspective? Is there anything particularly RESTful, or are there any unusual route configurations that warrant closer inspection?

`app/` is the beating heart. I need to understand the architecture within the app directory. Are we dealing with the Model-View-Controller framework, or something more advanced? Are there any patterns? Are there any service layers, decorators, or concerns that I should be aware of? Are we talking about a monolith or a system with a lot of microservices? I need to build a mental map of what's inside to avoid confusion later.

`test/` tells me about the quality of the system and how the components interact. Are we talking about unit tests, integration tests, or end-to-end tests? The test suite provides a window into the developers' assumptions and the application's expected behavior. Any gaps in test coverage will be flagged for investigation later.

Finally, `Gemfile` offers a glimpse into the dependencies. What libraries are we leveraging? Anything particularly interesting? Are there any potential vulnerabilities or outdated versions that need attention? What are the core dependencies, and what are the auxiliary gems used for specific parts of the system?

Essentially, I'm performing a quick, in-depth scan of the repository to get my bearings. I want to build a comprehensive mental model before I get my hands dirty. It’s about creating the context I need to make informed decisions down the line.

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end
end

class Room::MessagePusher
  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(mentionees)
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)
    end

    def relevant_subscriptions
      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)
    end
end

      create!(attributes).tap(&:process_attachment)
    end
  end

  def attachment?

    ensure_attachment_analyzed
    process_attachment_thumbnail

module Membership::Connectable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  CONNECTION_TTL = 60.seconds

  included do
    scope :connected,    -> { where(connected_at: CONNECTION_TTL.ago..) }
    scope :disconnected, -> { where(connected_at: [ nil, ...CONNECTION_TTL.ago ]) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def disconnect_all
      connected.update_all connected_at: nil, connections: 0, updated_at: Time.current
    end

    def connect(membership, connections)
      where(id: membership.id).update_all(connections: connections, connected_at: Time.current, unread_at: nil)
    end
  end

  def connected?
    connected_at? && connected_at >= CONNECTION_TTL.ago
  end

  def present
    self.class.connect(self, connected? ? connections + 1 : 1)
  end

  def connected
    increment_connections
    touch :connected_at
  end

  def disconnected
    decrement_connections
    update! connected_at: nil if connections < 1
  end

  def refresh_connection
    increment_connections unless connected?
    touch :connected_at
  end

  def increment_connections
    connected? ? increment!(:connections, touch: true) : update!(connections: 1)
  end

  def decrement_connections
    connected? ? decrement!(:connections, touch: true) : update!(connections: 0)
  end
end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception
  end

  class_methods do
    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
    end

    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end
end

class RoomsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_room, only: %i[ show destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ destroy ]
  before_action :remember_last_room_visited, only: :show

  def index
    redirect_to room_url(Current.user.rooms.last)
  end

  def show
    @messages = find_messages
  end

  def destroy
    @room.destroy

    broadcast_remove_room
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def set_room
      if room = room_scope.find_by(id: params[:room_id] || params[:id])
        @room = room
      else
        redirect_to root_url, alert: "Room not found or inaccessible"
      end
    end

    # Subclasses narrow this to the room types they're allowed to act on, so that one
    # room namespace can't be used to reach another's rooms.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@room)
    end

    def ensure_permission_to_create_rooms
      if Current.account.settings.restrict_room_creation_to_administrators? && !Current.user.administrator?
        head :forbidden
      end
    end

    def find_messages
      messages = @room.messages.with_creator.with_attachment_details.with_boosts

      if show_first_message = messages.find_by(id: params[:message_id])
        @messages = messages.page_around(show_first_message)
      else
        @messages = messages.last_page
      end
    end

    def room_params
      params.require(:room).permit(:name)
    end

    def broadcast_remove_room
      broadcast_remove_to :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ]
    end
end

      [ author.name, author.bio ].compact_blank.join(" – ")

require "surfguard"

module RestrictedHTTP
  class Violation < StandardError; end

  # The address policy lives in the surfguard gem so this app, Basecamp, HEY and
  # Fizzy classify "internal" the same way instead of each keeping a copy that
  # drifts. The callers here hand a bare hostname in and pin the address that
  # comes back, so this stays a hostname-in, address-out shim.
  module PrivateNetworkGuard
    extend self

    # A hostname that resolves to nothing (NXDOMAIN, timeout, empty answer)
    # raises Surfguard::Unresolvable, which we let propagate as a lookup failure
    # -- the same way the old Resolv.getaddress guard raised Resolv::ResolvError,
    # and the callers here already treat it as a fetch failure. The Violation is
    # reserved for a host that resolves to a blocked address (an empty list back
    # from resolve_public_ips), so a transient DNS miss is never misreported as
    # an SSRF attempt.
    def resolve(hostname)
      Surfguard.resolve_public_ips(hostname).first or
        raise Violation.new("Attempt to access private IP via #{hostname}")
    end

    def private_ip?(ip)
      Surfguard.blocked_address?(ip)
    end
  end
end

# This is in lib so we can use it in a thread pool without the Rails executor
class WebPush::Pool
  attr_reader :delivery_pool, :invalidation_pool, :connection, :invalid_subscription_handler

  def initialize(invalid_subscription_handler:)
    @delivery_pool = Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor.new(max_threads: 50, queue_size: 10000)
    @invalidation_pool = Concurrent::FixedThreadPool.new(1)
    @connection = Net::HTTP::Persistent.new(name: "web_push", pool_size: 150)
    @invalid_subscription_handler = invalid_subscription_handler
  end

  def queue(payload, subscriptions)
    subscriptions.find_each do |subscription|
      deliver_later(payload, subscription)
    end
  end

  def shutdown
    connection.shutdown
    shutdown_pool(delivery_pool)
    shutdown_pool(invalidation_pool)
  end

  private
    def deliver_later(payload, subscription)
      # Ensure any AR operations happen before we post to the thread pool
      notification = subscription.notification(**payload)
      subscription_id = subscription.id

      delivery_pool.post do
        deliver(notification, subscription_id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.deliver: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    rescue Concurrent::RejectedExecutionError
    end

    def deliver(notification, id)
      notification.deliver(connection: connection)
    rescue WebPush::ExpiredSubscription, OpenSSL::OpenSSLError => ex
      invalidate_subscription_later(id) if invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    def invalidate_subscription_later(id)
      invalidation_pool.post do
        invalid_subscription_handler.call(id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.invalid_subscription_handler: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    end

    def shutdown_pool(pool)
      pool.shutdown
      pool.kill unless pool.wait_for_termination(1)
    end
end

**A Deep Dive into Bot Deletion**

Okay, here's the breakdown, starting with a crucial observation: we need to understand what happens when a bot gets "deleted." The prompt is very specific: "A deleted bot can no longer post messages." This isn't just about removing the user, it's about *preventing future messages*. We are using Campfire's deletion pattern from `Accounts::UsersController#destroy` which calls `@user.deactivate`.

The critical question, as I see it, is the difference between *deactivating* a bot and *destroying* it in the database. `User` has `has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy`, which means destroying the user would delete all associated messages. But the wording in the prompt leads me to think that we will be calling `@bot.deactivate`.

Let's look at `User#deactivate` and trace it:
*   `status` becomes `:deactivated`. This means our bot is no longer `active?` and is therefore no longer found when calling `User.active`.
*   Direct rooms are unaffected because direct rooms are not being deleted.
*   This deactivation removes the bot from the `/bots` list, and prevents it from being edited.
*   The bot's `bot_token` will be set to `nil` (or checked for the `active?` flag), so our bot's credentials are no longer valid. When a bot tries to use its `bot_code`, the server will now return a `401 Unauthorized` error.
*   *Crucially*, the messages the bot *already* posted remain in the chat history. They are not destroyed, or removed! These messages are critical for logging, documentation, and the history of deployments!

Let's test all these assumptions with:
1.  A bot is created, named "Deploy Bot".
2.  The bot is listed on `/bots`.
3.  We post messages with the bot's code and can see messages in the room.
4.  Edit "Deploy Bot" -> click "Delete this chat bot" -> confirm -> redirect to `/bots` -> "Deploy Bot" is gone.
5.  If we try to post messages with the "deleted" bot code -> `401 Unauthorized`.
6.  The existing message from "Deploy Bot" in step 3 remains in the room, showing the bot's name and avatar.

Therefore, deleting a bot *should not* destroy associated messages. `User#deactivate` is the desired behavior, which we get from `Accounts::UsersController#destroy`.

Now, let's look at how the `email_address` is handled. We see the `email_address&.gsub(...)` in `deactivate`. Why? Because bots don't have email addresses. This pattern allows us to deactivate the user in a consistent way.

Finally, we also see the database design and tests are also in line with this behavior. We have not made `password_digest` nullable as bot users do not need a password, and the tests should be written in this style. This confirms that this deletion is consistent with all tests and is secure.

require "application_system_test_case"

class SendingMessagesTest < ApplicationSystemTestCase
  setup do
    sign_in "jz@37signals.com"
    join_room rooms(:designers)
  end

  test "sending messages between two users" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)
    end

    join_room rooms(:designers)
    send_message "Is this thing on?"

    using_session("Kevin") do
      join_room rooms(:designers)
      assert_message_text "Is this thing on?"

      send_message "👍👍"
    end

    join_room rooms(:designers)
    assert_message_text "👍👍"
  end

  test "editing messages" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)
    end

    within_message messages(:third) do
      reveal_message_actions
      find(".message__edit-btn").click
      fill_in_rich_text_area "message_body", with: "Redacted!"
      click_on "Save changes"
    end

    using_session("Kevin") do
      join_room rooms(:designers)

      assert_message_text "Redacted!"
    end
  end

  test "deleting messages" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)

      assert_message_text "Third time's a charm."
    end

    within_message messages(:third) do
      reveal_message_actions
      find(".message__edit-btn").click

      accept_confirm do
        click_on "Delete message"
      end
    end

    using_session("Kevin") do
      assert_message_text "Third time's a charm.", count: 0
    end
  end
end

Okay, here's the breakdown, starting with a crucial observation: the `app/views/users/new.html.erb` file saved us from a potential nightmare scenario. The solution found in `app/views/users/new.html.erb` involves a single form containing the avatar `<input type="file">` inside a `<label>` (leveraging `upload-preview`) and the name `<input type="text">`, all submitted together with a button. This one-form approach avoids the problems of premature submission or overwrite issues.

Now, let's nail down every detail of the shared `app/views/bots/_form.html.erb` partial, ensuring we cover bot creation *and* editing:

1.  **Form URL and Model:** We need to confirm the form's target URL and model. By using `form_with model: bot, scope: :bot, url: bot.new_record? ? bots_path : bot_path(bot)`, we ensure that on `/bots/new`, it posts to `/bots` and on `/bots/:id/edit`, it patches `/bots/:id`.  The field names will correctly be `bot[avatar]` and `bot[name]`. The controller will use  `params.require(:bot).permit(:name, :avatar)`, a Campfire standard, ensuring consistent parameter handling.

2.  **Avatar Field:** The avatar image preview mechanism is the key element here. The crucial point is the presence of *only one* `<input type="file">` inside a `<label>`. This prevents the ambiguity that can arise if there were multiple file inputs, and it enables the preview using `upload-preview`. The use of `bot.persisted?` handles the display of either the uploaded avatar, the initials SVG, or the default avatar image correctly. `Users::AvatarsController#show` is designed to show the uploaded 512x512 WebP avatar (if available), or the initials SVG. Here is the *critical* optimization catch: ActiveStorage, by default, doesn't touch the owner model's `updated_at` when only the `avatar` changes, which breaks the ETag cache, so we need to call `@bot.touch` *on update* to ensure the avatar updates are correctly reflected. This updates the `updated_at` attribute, invalidating the ETag and forcing a fresh avatar retrieval. This is a vital performance optimization!

3.  **Bot Name Field:**  We're making sure the bot name field meets all requirements.  Specifically, The `<label>` element's text *should* match the `placeholder`, `aria-label`, and screen reader text ("Name the bot"). Also, the input *must* have `required: true`. We **MUST** add `validates :name, presence: true, if: :bot?` in `app/models/user.rb` (scoped by `bot?`) to enforce server-side validation.

4.  **"Save Changes" Button:** The button must use the exact style of `btn btn--reversed center txt-large`. This style includes `check.svg` image and the screen reader text "Save changes". This will ensure the button is properly located by tests like the other Campfire buttons.

5.  **"Delete This Chat Bot" Button:** The delete button, displayed on the edit page, has to utilize the native browser `confirm()` dialog. The code should use `data: { turbo_confirm: "Are you sure you want to delete this chat bot?" }`, which triggers a native confirmation dialog, and the button's text is `"Delete this chat bot"` to match test expectations.

steps.reasoning_content:
**Deep Dive into Bot API Endpoint Implementation**

Okay, let's break this down. First, regarding the bot management forms, I need to make a few things explicitly clear. `Turbo.setConfirmMethod` doesn't override the `data: { turbo_confirm: "..." }` attribute, so the default browser `confirm()` dialog is used. Crucially, the `button_to` element, used for delete actions, must be generated *outside* the main edit form (`form_with`). It's best practice to place this outside the form tag to prevent nested forms which are invalid HTML and cause issues in Turbo. I can place it in a separate `<section>` or below the form render, like in the `rooms/layouts/_edit.html.erb` example.  Both forms should work independently this way.  Also, after a successful `DELETE` or `PATCH` request for bots, the redirection target *must* be `/bots` -  `bots_url`.  The spec dictates this, as the bot management page (`/bots`) is the central point for both create, update, and delete operations. It's the only page where these functions are performed.

Now, let's dive into the core of the problem: the bot's HTTP API. I'm going to meticulously analyze the `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` endpoint. Every single detail matters.

When a `curl` request, such as `curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" ...`, is sent, I need to understand *exactly* what's going on at the HTTP level.  This is a critical area.

Specifically, I've got to carefully consider:

1.  **Content-Type**: By default, `curl -d` sends `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. That's important because Rails will interpret the request body accordingly.
2.  **User-Agent**: `curl` sends `User-Agent: curl/8.x.x`. I have to check the `AllowBrowser` concern in `ApplicationController`. Does it block `curl` or potentially old browser User-Agents from scripts? I'll probably need to skip `allow_browser` or implement a specific check.
3.  **CSRF Protection**:  Since `curl` doesn't send a CSRF token or session cookie, I *must* skip CSRF protection. So, `skip_forgery_protection` is required for this controller (and I'll allow unauthenticated access via the `bot_key`).
4.  **Request Body Handling**: Now, the crucial part: What do `request.raw_post` and `request.body.read` return in Rails when `Content-Type` is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`? If Rack has already read the body, `request.body.read` might return an empty string unless `request.body.rewind` is called, or I use `request.raw_post` directly. Moreover, and this is *absolutely key*, `request.raw_post` returns a string with `ASCII-8BIT` (aka `Encoding::BINARY`) encoding.  The request body contains UTF-8 characters! Now, if that binary string with an emoji, like the example's `✅`, is passed to ActionText, ERB, or ActiveRecord *without* proper encoding conversion via `.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)` (or similar), a nasty `Encoding::CompatibilityError` will be raised. That emoji is why this is in the prompt! I'll test it right now in the Rails runner!

This is a critical consideration for a production bot API! I'm going to make *absolutely certain* that the encoding is handled correctly to avoid silent data corruption or, worse, errors.

steps.reasoning_content:
**Deep Dive into Browser Compatibility and Message Creation** Okay, so I'm looking at how we're handling browser compatibility and message creation for bots, and I'm seeing some interesting possibilities. First, that `AllowBrowser` concern in `app/controllers/concerns/allow_browser.rb` could be *really* clean. If we're using Rails 8's `allow_browser versions: ..., only: ...` or something similar, we can easily block specific browser versions based on the User-Agent string. But what if a headless script sends a malformed User-Agent? We need to ensure these checks don't interfere with bot functionality. The beauty of the `AllowBrowser` setup, especially if we can use an `if: :enforce_browser_versions?` approach with a clear `allow_all_browsers` method, is we can easily override the browser checks. We can even do this in `Messages::ByBotsController` by using `skip_browser_check` or setting `self.browser_check_enabled = false`, making it inherit everything without the compatibility checks. That's a good pattern and a nice example of Rails-omakase. So, let's look at `Messages::ByBotsController#create`... this is where things get interesting. I'm going to trace every single line of this, and test the edge cases. First, a normal scenario using curl with the right bot key, room ID, and a simple message body. It authenticates, finds the room, and the message gets created. The `formatted_body` method is important here. It's properly escaping the text before saving it, ensuring there's no HTML injection. We'll broadcast the message and return a 201 Created. So far so good. Next, I need to test edge cases where the message body might be empty, or contain HTML content. Empty body? Validation fails, and we get a 422. Blank body, same result. So we have to test edge cases! * Empty body and no attachment: 422 Unprocessable Content! * `curl -d " \n\t " .../rooms///messages` -> `raw.blank?` is `true` -> `formatted_body` is `""` -> `422 Unprocessable Content`! * `curl -H "Content-Type: text/html" -d "

"` -> `body.blank?` is `true` -> `422 Unprocessable Content`! * `curl -H "Content-Type: text/html" -d ""` -> WAIT A SECOND! Wait, sending HTML content using the POST request, what's our policy on the bot request! It's supposed to be raw text! When we escape the raw body to create the text body of a message, are we escaping raw HTML? We are, by using `ERB::Util.html_escape(raw).gsub(/\r?\n/, "
")`! But why do we allow `Content-Type: text/html` at all when the instructions say "Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names."? We *could* just hard-code the content type, but then it becomes harder to test. This is critical. If we escape HTML when the content type is *not* `text/html`, then: * Bots can *never* inject raw HTML tags, or spoof any tags. * Any non-blank text is displayed as text! * URLs are still auto-linked, and *safe*! Therefore, we *must* ensure HTML is escaped. We need to be confident that `` is *safely* escaped. That way, any non-HTML format is 100% safe.

**Caching Nirvana Achieved!**

Whoa, hold on a second! Just taking a look at `config/environments/production.rb`, and there it is: `config.action_controller.perform_caching = true`. Okay, and then I'm in `app/views/messages/_message.html.erb`... check it out: `<% cache [ message, "presentation-v2" ] do %>`. The gears are turning. If our QA environment is set up like production (or, you know, caching is just enabled), and someone edits a bot's name or avatar *after* it's already posted, that old bot info is going to be stubbornly hanging around in cached fragments if that `message` object isn't invalidated or updated in the cache key.

So, initial thoughts are around something like `BotsController#update` or a relevant callback like `User::Bot`'s `after_update_commit`, or... wait... how about `cache [ message, message.creator, "presentation-v2" ]`? No, no, hold on, `MessagesController` is already using `messages.with_creator`, so `message.creator` is *already* preloaded on every message! That's a key detail! Okay, maybe an `@bot.messages.touch_all` on bot update?

Wait a minute, let's compare that `@bot.messages.touch_all` approach in `BotsController#update` to just modifying that `_message.html.erb` file.

Now I see it! Look at this, this `@bot.messages.touch_all` on bot update... the genius of it is:
1)  We don't even have to mess with `_message.html.erb`'s cache key for all human messages!
2) Updating a bot (using `BotsController#update`) does `touch` on the `@bot` object, AND it does `@bot.messages.touch_all` which will bust BOTH `fresh_user_avatar_path(@bot)` AND `stale?(etag: @user)` AND `fresh_when @messages` in `MessagesController#index` AND `Rooms::RefreshesController` AND `[ message, "presentation-v2" ]` fragment cache!!

That's brilliant! One single line of code, `@bot.messages.touch_all`, invalidates *all* of those things: HTTP ETags, room refreshes, avatar URLs, AND fragment caches! It's so elegant.

Okay, next step: let's make sure `bin/rubocop` is passing without any offenses. Got to keep it clean. Our `.rubocop.yml` is already using `rubocop-rails-omakase`, so let's check it before we get carried away.

require "test_helper"

class User::BotTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.user = users(:kevin)
  end

  test "creating a bot generates a unique bot_key and grants membership to open rooms" do
    bot = nil
    assert_difference -> { Membership.count }, +Rooms::Open.count do
      bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")
    end

    assert bot.bot?
    assert bot.active?
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert bot.bot_token.present?
    assert_equal "#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}", bot.bot_key
    assert_equal Rooms::Open.all.sort, bot.rooms.sort
  end

  test "bot requires a name" do
    bot = User.new(role: :bot, name: "")
    assert_not bot.valid?
  end

  test "human users do not get a bot_token" do
    user = User.create!(name: "Human", email_address: "human@example.com", password: "secret123456")
    assert_nil user.bot_token
    assert_nil user.bot_key
  end

  test "authenticate_bot validates active bots and rejects invalid or deactivated bots" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")
    key = bot.bot_key

    assert_equal bot, User.authenticate_bot(key)
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}-wrongtoken")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("999999-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("invalid")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(nil)

    bot.deactivate
    assert bot.reload.deactivated?
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(key)
  end
end
EOF

require "test_helper"

class BotsControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  test "account edit page shows Set up chat bots link to both members and admins" do
    sign_in :kevin

    assert_response :success
    assert_select "a[href='#{bots_path}']", text: /Set up chat bots/

    sign_in :david
    get edit_account_url
    assert_response :success
    assert_select "a[href='#{bots_path}']", text: /Set up chat bots/
  end

  test "members see only their own bots without pagination while admins see all bots" do
    kevin_bot = User.bots.create!(name: "Kevin Bot", creator: users(:kevin))
    jz_bot = User.bots.create!(name: "JZ Bot", creator: users(:jz))

    sign_in :kevin
    get bots_url
    assert_response :success
    assert_select "a[href='#{new_bot_path}']", text: /Add a chat bot/
    assert_select "li", text: /Kevin Bot/ do
      assert_select "input[readonly][value='#{kevin_bot.bot_key}']"
      assert_select "a[href='#{edit_bot_path(kevin_bot)}']", text: /Edit Kevin Bot/
    end
    assert_select "li", text: /JZ Bot/, count: 0

    sign_in :david
    get bots_url
    assert_response :success
    assert_select "li", text: /Kevin Bot/
    assert_select "li", text: /JZ Bot/
  end

  test "member can create edit and delete their own bot" do
    sign_in :kevin

    get new_bot_url
    assert_response :success
    assert_select "input[placeholder='Name the bot'][required]"
    assert_select "button[type='submit']", text: /Save changes/

    assert_difference -> { User.active_bots.count }, +1 do
      post bots_url, params: { bot: { name: "Deploy Bot", avatar: fixture_file_upload("moon.jpg", "image/jpeg") } }
    end
    assert_redirected_to bots_url

    bot = User.active_bots.last
    assert_equal "Deploy Bot", bot.name
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert bot.avatar.attached?

    get edit_bot_url(bot)
    assert_response :success
    assert_select "button", text: /Delete this chat bot/

    patch bot_url(bot), params: { bot: { name: "Renamed Bot", avatar: "" } }
    assert_redirected_to bots_url
    assert_equal "Renamed Bot", bot.reload.name
    assert bot.avatar.attached?, "Updating name without new avatar should preserve existing avatar"

    assert_difference -> { User.active_bots.count }, -1 do
      delete bot_url(bot)
    end
    assert_redirected_to bots_url
    assert bot.reload.deactivated?
  end

  test "member cannot edit update or delete another member's bot" do

    assert_response :forbidden

    patch bot_url(jz_bot), params: { bot: { name: "Hacked" } }
    assert_response :forbidden

    delete bot_url(jz_bot)

    assert_redirected_to bots_url

end

cat <<'EOF' > test/controllers/messages/by_bots_controller_test.rb
require "test_helper"

class Messages::ByBotsControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup do
    host! "once.campfire.test"
    @bot = User.bots.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin))
    @open_room = rooms(:hq)
  end

  test "bot posts raw body to open room and broadcasts and enqueues push notifications" do
    assert_difference -> { @open_room.messages.count }, +1 do
      assert_enqueued_jobs 1, only: [ Room::PushMessageJob ] do
        assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast @open_room, :messages, action: "append", target: [ @open_room, :messages ] do
          post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages",
            params: "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅",
            headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }

          assert_response :created
          message = Message.last
          assert_equal "/messages/#{message.id}", response.headers["Location"]
          assert_equal @bot, message.creator
          assert_equal "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅", message.plain_text_body

          assert_select ".message__author", text: "Deploy Bot"
          assert_select ".message__body", text: /Deploy of v1\.2\.3 finished ✅/
        end
      end
    end
  end

  test "returns 422 on empty body and no attachment" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: ""
      assert_response :unprocessable_content

      post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "   \n  "
      assert_response :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  test "returns 404 on bad room id or room the bot is not a member of" do
    post "/rooms/999999/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello"
    assert_response :not_found

    closed_room = rooms(:designers)
    assert_not closed_room.users.include?(@bot)
    post "/rooms/#{closed_room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello"
    assert_response :not_found
  end

  test "bot added to closed room can post messages to it" do
    closed_room = rooms(:designers)
    closed_room.memberships.grant_to(@bot)

    post "/rooms/#{closed_room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Design deploy ready"
    assert_response :created
  end

  test "returns 401 on invalid bot code or deleted bot" do
    post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/invalid-code/messages", params: "Hello"
    assert_response :unauthorized

    post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/invalid.code/messages", params: "Hello"
    assert_response :unauthorized

    post "/rooms/999999/invalid-code/messages", params: "Hello"
    assert_response :unauthorized

    bot_key = @bot.bot_key
    @bot.deactivate

    post "/rooms/#{@open_room.id}/#{bot_key}/messages", params: "After deletion"
    assert_response :unauthorized
  end
end
EOF

steps.reasoning_content:
**Model and Configuration Updates**

Alright, time to roll up my sleeves and get these model and configuration updates deployed. I need to carefully review the `User::Role`, `User::Bot`, `User`, and `Message` models before I start making changes to the code itself, as well as the `filter_parameter_logging.rb` and `routes.rb` files.

First, the `User::Role` module is pretty straightforward. I'm seeing the use of `ActiveSupport::Concern` to extend the user model and an enum to define the user roles: member, administrator, and bot. I note the `can_administer?` method checks both administrator status and creator status if applicable.

Next, `User::Bot` is where things get a bit more interesting. This module handles bot-specific functionality using `ActiveSupport::Concern`, defining associations, scopes to handle finding and filtering bots, and validations. The inclusion of `before_create :generate_bot_token, if: :bot?` and methods like `create_bot!` and `authenticate_bot` indicate a focus on creating and authenticating these bot accounts, which I'll have to consider as a core piece of this update. I pay close attention to the `bot_key` method because it includes a conditional check for `bot? && bot_token.present?`, which is a neat way to handle deactivated bots by returning nil if the `bot_token` is nil.

Moving on to the `User` model (`app/models/user.rb`), I have to double check the module inclusion order. I have to make sure that the `Role` module gets included *before* `Bot`, which is crucial for the correct behavior of the enum. This is a common gotcha, so I'm glad I caught it before making an error. Then, the `User#deactivate` method removes the bot_token if it exists.

Finally, the `Message` model (`app/models/message.rb`) introduces validation to ensure that a message has either a body or an attachment, which makes sense. I see the method `ensure_body_or_attachment_present`, which will validate this.

Okay, I've got a handle on the changes. Time to get these updates implemented.

arguments.command:
cat <<'EOF' > app/models/user/role.rb
module User::Role
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]
  end

  def can_administer?(record = nil)
    administrator? || self == record&.creator || record&.new_record?
  end
end
EOF

cat <<'EOF' > app/models/user/bot.rb
module User::Bot
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true
    has_many :bots, -> { active.bots }, class_name: "User", foreign_key: :creator_id

    scope :bots, -> { where(role: :bot) }
    scope :without_bots, -> { where.not(role: :bot) }
    scope :active_bots, -> { active.bots }

    before_create :generate_bot_token, if: :bot?

    validates :name, presence: true, if: :bot?
  end

  class_methods do
    def create_bot!(attributes)
      bots.create!({ creator: Current.user }.merge(attributes))
    end

    def authenticate_bot(bot_key)
      bot_id, bot_token = bot_key.to_s.split("-", 2)
      if bot_id.present? && bot_token.present? && (bot = active_bots.find_by(id: bot_id))
        bot if ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(bot.bot_token, bot_token)
      end
    end
  end

  def bot_key
    "#{id}-#{bot_token}" if bot? && bot_token.present?
  end

  private
    def generate_bot_token
      self.bot_token ||= self.class.generate_unique_secure_token
    end
end
EOF

class User < ApplicationRecord

  has_many :reachable_messages, through: :rooms, source: :messages
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :creator_id

  has_many :push_subscriptions, class_name: "Push::Subscription", dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :booster_id
  has_many :searches, dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :bans, dependent: :destroy

  enum :status, %i[ active deactivated banned ], default: :active

  has_secure_password validations: false

  after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }
  scope :filtered_by, ->(query) { where("name like ?", "%#{query}%") }

  def initials
    name.scan(/\b\w/).join
  end

  def title
    [ name, bio ].compact_blank.join(" – ")
  end

  def deactivate
    transaction do
      close_remote_connections

      memberships.without_direct_rooms.delete_all
      push_subscriptions.delete_all
      searches.delete_all
      sessions.delete_all

      update! status: :deactivated, email_address: deactived_email_address, bot_token: nil
    end
  end

  def reset_remote_connections
    close_remote_connections reconnect: true
  end

  private
    def grant_membership_to_open_rooms
      Membership.insert_all(Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).collect { |room_id| { room_id: room_id, user_id: id } })
    end

    def deactived_email_address
      email_address&.gsub(/@/, "-deactivated-#{SecureRandom.uuid}@")
    end

    def close_remote_connections(reconnect: false)
      ActionCable.server.remote_connections.where(current_user: self).disconnect reconnect: reconnect
    end
end
EOF

class Message < ApplicationRecord
  include Attachment, Broadcasts, Mentionee, Pagination, Searchable

  belongs_to :room, touch: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy

  has_rich_text :body

  validate :ensure_body_or_attachment_present

  before_create -> { self.client_message_id ||= Random.uuid }
  after_create_commit -> { room.receive(self) }

  scope :ordered, -> { order(:created_at) }
  scope :with_creator, -> { preload(creator: :avatar_attachment) }
  scope :with_attachment_details, -> {
    with_rich_text_body_and_embeds
    with_attached_attachment
      .includes(attachment_blob: :variant_records)
  }
  scope :with_boosts, -> { includes(boosts: :booster) }

  def plain_text_body
    body.to_plain_text.presence || attachment&.filename&.to_s || ""
  end

  def to_key
    [ client_message_id ]
  end

  def content_type
    case
    when attachment?    then "attachment"
    when sound.present? then "sound"
    else                     "text"
    end.inquiry
  end

  def sound
    plain_text_body.match(/\A\/play (?<name>\w+)\z/) do |match|
      Sound.find_by_name match[:name]
    end
  end

  private
    def ensure_body_or_attachment_present
      if body.blank? && !attachment?
        errors.add(:body, :blank)
      end
    end
end

**Controller and View Creation Time!**

Okay, let's get down to brass tacks. Time to build out these controllers and views. I need to create `AllowBrowser`, `BotsController`, `Messages::ByBotsController`, and update `AccountsController`, `Accounts::UsersController`, `SessionsController`, `Sessions::TransfersController`, and `Users::BansController`. And, of course, the views: `bot.svg`, `accounts/edit.html.erb`, `users/show.html.erb`, `bots/index.html.erb`, `bots/_bot.html.erb`, `bots/new.html.erb`, `bots/edit.html.erb`, and `bots/_form.html.erb`.

Wait a second. Before I get too far ahead of myself, let's just double-check that `Users::BansController`. Yep, that `before_action :set_user` in `app/controllers/users/bans_controller.rb` is exactly what I was hoping to see. Using `.without_bots` within that `set_user` method to prevent a bot from being banned and returning a 404 is a beautifully clean solution. Elegant.

Now, let's take a quick look at `BotsController#update`. Interesting. The `@bot.touch` and `@bot.messages.touch_all` calls are brilliant. Even if only the avatar changes, that `@bot.updated_at` change will trigger a new `?v=` on `fresh_user_avatar_path(@bot)`, and `Users::AvatarsController`'s `stale?(etag: @user)` will serve the new avatar. The `@bot.messages.touch_all` is even better! Updating the `updated_at` on any messages authored by `@bot` will bust those fragment caches. That means the `[ message, "presentation-v2" ]` and `Rooms::RefreshesController` (`page_updated_since`) will see the change. Perfect, a robust cache invalidation strategy.

Alright, with these checks in place, let's get those controllers, the SVG, and all those views written!

Essentially, when `show_exceptions` is set to `:none` in the test environment, any controller *without* explicit `rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` will raise the `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` exception directly within an `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest`. Unlike development or production, where this exception is gracefully converted to a 404 response by ActionDispatch, in the test environment it just pops out. Notice, though, that `Messages::ByBotsController` is *already* handling this with `rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound, with: -> { head :not_found }`, which explains why it behaves as expected and returns a clean 404 even with this setting!

Adding `rescue_from(ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound) { head :not_found }` to `BotsController` now fixes this issue. So, a `get edit_bot_url(non_existent_or_deactivated)` call will return a clean 404 in both test and production environments.

And, regarding that `test_bots_cannot_be_accessed_via_human_user_admin_or_login_endpoints` test, I see that the `assert_raises(ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound)` test in `Accounts::UsersController` relies on Rails' exception wrapper so should function correctly.

Now, let's shift gears to the `User::BotTest#test_converting_a_closed_room_to_an_open_room_grants_membership_to_active_bots` test. Here's a subtle point that I think is important. Initially, `closed_room` was a `Rooms::Closed` instance. After `closed_room.becomes!(Rooms::Open).save!`, the `type` column in the database is updated to `"Rooms::Open"`. Using `Room.find(closed_room.id).users.include?(bot)` is what correctly reloads it as `Rooms::Open`.

steps.message: Let's run `bin/rails runner` in the foreground first so `/tmp/bot_test_info.txt` is written before starting the server and running `curl`.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Debugging a Pesky Shell Command**

Right, okay, I see it now! The reason `ROOM_ID` and `BOT_CODE` were coming up empty in that `POST "/rooms/messages"` request (and consequently hitting the `MessagesController#create` action) is because of that dang shell command. Specifically, the way I was running `bin/rails runner '...' && bin/rails server ... &`. The entire pipeline, including the part that writes to `/tmp/bot_test_info.txt`, was being thrown into the background with the `&`! So, the `ROOM_ID=$(sed ...)` command was executing *before* the information was even written to the file. Classic race condition.

The fix is straightforward. I need to force the `bin/rails runner` task to complete *before* `bin/rails server` starts. I'll switch from the background process (`&& ... &`) to running them sequentially in the foreground by using a semicolon: `bin/rails runner ... ; bin/rails server &`. That should do the trick! Let's see if this gives us the clean responses we need to analyze, those crisp `201 Created`, `422 Unprocessable Content`, `404 Not Found`, and `401 Unauthorized` headers... Let's get this test running!

arguments.command:
redis-server --port 6379 --daemonize no >/tmp/redis_test.log 2>&1 &
REDIS_PID=$!
sleep 0.3

bin/rails runner '
  user = FirstRun.create!(name: "Admin", email_address: "admin@example.com", password: "secret123456")
  room = Room.first
  bot = User.bots.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: user)
  File.write("/tmp/bot_test_info.txt", "#{room.id}\n#{bot.bot_key}\n")
'

bin/rails server -p 4567 -b 127.0.0.1 >/tmp/puma_test.log 2>&1 &
PUMA_PID=$!
trap "kill $PUMA_PID $REDIS_PID 2>/dev/null || true; rm -f /tmp/bot_test_info.txt /tmp/puma_test.log /tmp/redis_test.log tmp/pids/server.pid dump.rdb" EXIT
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  if curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:4567/up >/dev/null 2>&1; then break; fi
  sleep 0.3
done

ROOM_ID=$(sed -n '1p' /tmp/bot_test_info.txt)
BOT_CODE=$(sed -n '2p' /tmp/bot_test_info.txt)

echo "=== 201 Created ==="
curl -s -D - -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" "http://127.0.0.1:4567/rooms/${ROOM_ID}/${BOT_CODE}/messages"
echo "=== 422 Empty ==="
curl -s -D - -d "" "http://127.0.0.1:4567/rooms/${ROOM_ID}/${BOT_CODE}/messages"
echo "=== 404 Bad Room ==="
curl -s -D - -d "Deploy" "http://127.0.0.1:4567/rooms/999999/${BOT_CODE}/messages"
echo "=== 401 Bad Bot Code ==="
curl -s -D - -d "Deploy" "http://127.0.0.1:4567/rooms/${ROOM_ID}/wrong-code/messages"

kill $PUMA_PID $REDIS_PID 2>/dev/null || true
wait $PUMA_PID $REDIS_PID 2>/dev/null || true
bin/rails db:schema:load

steps.message: Let's reset `storage/db/development.sqlite3*` cleanly with `bin/rails db:migrate` and run the live `curl` test!
steps.reasoning_content:
**A Database Mystery**

Okay, hold on a minute! The live server test just threw an error: `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` with a `SQLite3::ConstraintException: constraint failed` within `Message::Searchable#create_in_index`... specifically on an `insert into message_search_index` statement! What's going on here?

Let's think. In the previous run, before Redis was running, `Message#create!` managed to commit the `Message` with id=1 *and* insert a row with `rowid=1` into `message_search_index` *before* the `broadcast_create` choked on that `Redis::CannotConnectError`! The problem is, then `bin/rails db:schema:load` came along and dropped and recreated the regular tables like `messages`. Crucially, because the `create_virtual_table` in `db/schema.rb` uses `IF NOT EXISTS` (or the FTS5 shadow tables weren't dropped!), the virtual table, `message_search_index`, was *not* dropped. Thus, it *still* had that `rowid=1` from the previous run. That's why the insert failed on the current run!

To confirm this, let's run `bin/rails db:reset` or just delete the `storage/db/development.sqlite3` file and run `bin/rails db:migrate` again and re-run the live curl test to verify! Let's check this immediately!

  File.write("/tmp/bot_test_info.txt", "#{room.id}\n#{bot.bot_key}\n")
'

bin/rails server -p 4567 -b 127.0.0.1 >/tmp/puma_test.log 2>&1 &
PUMA_PID=$!
trap "kill $PUMA_PID $REDIS_PID 2>/dev/null || true; rm -f /tmp/bot_test_info.txt /tmp/puma_test.log /tmp/redis_test.log tmp/pids/server.pid dump.rdb" EXIT
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  if curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:4567/up >/dev/null 2>&1; then break; fi
  sleep 0.3
done

ROOM_ID=$(sed -n '1p' /tmp/bot_test_info.txt)
BOT_CODE=$(sed -n '2p' /tmp/bot_test_info.txt)

echo "=== 201 Created ==="
curl -s -D - -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" "http://127.0.0.1:4567/rooms/${ROOM_ID}/${BOT_CODE}/messages"
echo "=== 422 Empty ==="

steps.message:
I have implemented chat bots in Campfire along with UI management and the HTTP message posting API:

- **Model & Schema (`User::Bot`, `User::Role`, `Message`)**:
  - Extended `User` with a `:bot` role (`User::Bot` concern), nullable `password_digest`, a unique `bot_token` (`bot_key` formatted as `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"`), and `creator_id` ownership so `Current.user.can_administer?(bot)` works seamlessly for both bot creators and administrators.
  - New bots automatically join all open rooms (`Rooms::Open`) and can be added to closed or direct rooms the same way as human members, while human-only surfaces (`/account/edit` member list, interactive login, session transfers, bans) exclude bots via `User.without_bots`.
  - Deleting a bot deactivates it and clears its `bot_token`, preventing future API requests while keeping previously posted messages intact.
  - Added validation on `Message` requiring either a non-empty `body` or an `attachment`, and registered bot credential parameters in `config.filter_parameters`.

- **User Interface (`BotsController`, `/account/edit`, `/bots`, `/bots/new`, `/bots/:id/edit`)**:
  - Added the `"Set up chat bots"` icon button on `/account/edit` for all chat members.
  - Added `/bots` showing all of a member's active bots (or all active bots for administrators) on a single page without pagination, displaying each bot's name, read-only `"Bot code"` input, and `"Edit <bot name>"` link in the same list item, plus the `"Add a chat bot"` button.
  - Added `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` sharing the same form (`"Name the bot"`, optional avatar upload, `"Save changes"`), with `"Delete this chat bot"` using native browser confirmation (`data-turbo-confirm`) on the edit page.

- **Bot HTTP API (`Messages::ByBotsController`, `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages`)**:
  - Authenticates `<bot-code>` in constant time (`401 Unauthorized` when invalid or deleted), verifies room membership (`404 Not Found` on invalid/inaccessible room), validates content (`422 Unprocessable Content` when empty and without attachment), broadcasts messages and enqueues Web Push notifications identically to human messages, and responds with `201 Created` and `Location: /messages/:message_id`.

- **Documentation & Tests**:
  - Added architectural notes in `docs/bots.md` and unit/integration/browser-flow tests in `test/models/user/bot_test.rb`, `test/controllers/bots_controller_test.rb`, and `test/controllers/messages/by_bots_controller_test.rb`.
